title: Testing Web APIs with Postman and curl
description: Learn how to manually test Web API endpoints using Postman and the curl command-line tool.

data.text: Why Test APIs Manually?

Before you build a front-end or client application to consume a Web API, you need to be certain that the API itself works correctly. **Manual API testing** lets you send HTTP requests directly and inspect the raw response — status codes, headers, and body — without any client code getting in the way.

data.title: Two essential tools
data.text: **Postman** is a free desktop app with a visual interface for building and saving API requests. **curl** is a command-line tool available on every operating system. Both accomplish the same goal; Postman is friendlier for beginners, curl is faster for quick checks.
Prerequisites
Have your ASP.NET Core Web API project running locally. Note its URL — by default it will be something like `https://localhost:44324`. You will need this URL to target your API endpoints.
GET — Fetch All Reservations
The simplest test is a **GET** request. It requires no request body — only the URL. A successful call returns status **200 OK** and a JSON array of reservation objects.
Using Postman

data.title: Steps to test GET in Postman
items: Set the HTTP method dropdown to **GET**.
Inspect the response body — you should see a JSON array with the seed reservations.

data.text: Using curl

data.title: curl — GET all reservations
data.content: Run this command in a terminal pointed at your Web API project.

data.text: The `-s` flag silences curl's progress bar so you only see the response body. You should see the JSON array printed directly in your terminal.
GET by ID — Fetch a Single Record
To retrieve one reservation, append its `id` to the URL path. A valid ID returns **200 OK** with a single JSON object; an invalid or missing ID returns **400 Bad Request**.

data.title: curl — GET reservation with id = 2
data.content: Fetch a single reservation by its ID using curl.

data.text: POST — Create a New Reservation

A **POST** request sends new data to the server in the **request body**. The server creates a record and responds with the created object (usually with **201 Created**). The `Content-Type` header must be set to `application/json`.

data.title: curl — POST a new reservation
data.content: Create a new reservation by POSTing JSON data.

data.title: Content-Type header is required
data.text: Without -H "Content-Type: application/json", the API cannot parse the request body and will return 415 Unsupported Media Type.
PUT — Replace an Entire Reservation
A **PUT** request replaces the entire reservation. All fields should be included in the request body. The API returns the updated object with status **200 OK**.
PATCH — Partially Update a Reservation

**PATCH** is used when you only want to change specific fields, not the whole object. The server receives a JSON Patch document — a list of `op` (operation), `path`, and `value` entries. Set the `Content-Type` to `application/json-patch+json`.

data.title: curl — PATCH update one field
data.content: Change only the name of reservation #2.

data.text: DELETE — Remove a Reservation
A **DELETE** request requires only the resource URL. No body is needed. A successful delete typically returns **204 No Content**.

data.title: curl — DELETE reservation id 3
data.content: Permanently remove reservation #3 from the repository.

data.text: Inspecting the Response
Every API response has three parts you should check:

data.title: What to look at in any API response
items: **Status code** — confirms success (200/201/204) or indicates an error (400/401/404/500).
**Response headers** — especially Content-Type (should be application/json for JSON responses).
**Response body** — the actual data payload in JSON format.

data.title: Hands-on: Test Every Endpoint
data.description: With your Web API running, use curl or Postman to verify every CRUD endpoint. Record the status code and body you receive for each call.
steps: Run curl -s https://localhost:44324/api/Reservation and confirm you get a JSON array.
Run curl -s https://localhost:44324/api/Reservation/1 and confirm you get a single object.
POST a new reservation and note the returned id.
PATCH the reservation you just created to change only its name.
DELETE the reservation and confirm it is gone.
data.expectedOutcome: All five operations return the expected HTTP status codes and valid JSON bodies. You can read and explain every response.

items.text: GET /api/Reservation returns 200 with a JSON array.
GET /api/Reservation/1 returns a single reservation object.
items.hint: Try an invalid id to see a 400 response.

items.text: POST creates a reservation and returns 201 with the new object.
PATCH updates only the specified fields.
DELETE removes the reservation and returns 204.
